entities.name: Albert Rouet
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Albert Rouet (b. 1936) is a French cardinal and Archbishop Emeritus of Poitiers, known internationally for his innovative approach to parish reorganisation in an era of declining priestly vocations, which became known as the 'Poitiers model' and influenced Catholic pastoral planning worldwide. Born in Paris, he was ordained a priest and served in the Church of Paris before his appointment as Archbishop of Poitiers in 1994.

Facing a dramatic shortage of priests in his archdiocese, Rouet developed a radical reorganisation of parish life in the early 2000s: instead of maintaining empty parish structures run by increasingly overextended priests, he reorganised the diocese into larger ecclesial communities led by coordinating teams of lay people and deacons, with priests serving as sacramental ministers across multiple communities. This model—controversial in some circles but widely admired—attracted international attention as a potential template for Western dioceses facing similar demographic challenges.

Elevated to cardinal in 2010 by Pope Benedict XVI, Rouet became an internationally recognised voice on questions of ecclesial renewal, the role of the laity, and the future of the parish. His book 'Un Nouveau Visage d'Église' (A New Face of the Church) and other writings on ecclesiology reached wide audiences in the French-speaking Catholic world and beyond. He represents a form of French Catholic pastoral creativity that sought renewal from within without waiting for institutional permission.
